chapters.t: PART I — GEOTECHNICAL ENGINEERING (INCL. FOUNDATIONS & ADVANCED SOIL MECHANICS)

b: Soil: unconsolidated material formed by weathering of rocks (physical + chemical).
Residual soil: remains at place of formation (e.g. laterite).
Transported soils: alluvial (water), aeolian (wind), glacial (ice – till/drift), lacustrine (lake), marine (sea), colluvial (gravity – talus).
Black cotton soil: expansive clay rich in montmorillonite; large swell–shrink.
Laterite: residual, red due to iron oxide; tropical climates.
Bentonite: montmorillonite clay from volcanic ash; used in drilling mud and diaphragm walls.
Varved clay: alternate thin layers of silt and clay (glacial lakes).
Marl: calcareous clay. Caliche: soil cemented by calcium carbonate. Hardpan: dense cemented layer.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Soils of Pakistan: Indus plains — alluvial silts & sands (often loose, liquefiable, high water table); Potohar/Islamabad — silty clays & loess-like deposits; Karachi — marine clays and limestone; Thar & Cholistan — aeolian sands; northern areas — glacial/moraine deposits and boulders.
Weathering: Physical (temperature, frost, abrasion) gives coarse soils; chemical (oxidation, hydration, carbonation) gives clay minerals.
Loess (wind-blown silt) collapses on wetting; black cotton soil (montmorillonite) swells and shrinks; varved clays show alternate silt/clay layers (glacial lakes).

b: Weathering: in-place breakdown of rock. Erosion: removal and transport.
Physical: frost wedging (water expands ≈ 9% on freezing), exfoliation (onion-skin), thermal expansion, salt crystallisation.
Chemical: oxidation, hydration, hydrolysis (feldspar → kaolinite clay), carbonation (limestone dissolves), solution.
Chemical weathering dominant in hot humid climate; physical weathering in cold/arid climate.
Residual soil: formed in place. Transported soils: alluvial (river), lacustrine (lake), marine, aeolian/loess (wind), glacial/till (ice), colluvial/talus (gravity).
Soil profile: O (organic) → A (topsoil) → B (subsoil, accumulation) → C (weathered rock) → R (bedrock).
Three phases: solids, water, air. Dry and fully saturated soils are two-phase.
Void ratio e = Vv/Vs (can exceed 1). Porosity n = Vv/V (always < 1).
Degree of saturation S = Vw/Vv (0 dry, 1 saturated).
Air content ac = Va/Vv;  S + ac = 1.  Percentage air voids na = Va/V = n·ac.
Dry unit weight γd = Gγw/(1+e) = γ/(1+w).
Submerged unit weight γ′ = γsat − γw = (G−1)γw/(1+e)  (≈ half of γsat).
Specific gravity G: sands ≈ 2.65; clays 2.7–2.8; organic soils lower. Pycnometer (coarse), density bottle (fine).
Relative density Dr = (emax − e)/(emax − emin) × 100 = [(γd − γdmin)/(γdmax − γdmin)]·(γdmax/γd) × 100.
Dr classes: very loose 0–15, loose 15–35, medium 35–65, dense 65–85, very dense 85–100%.
Water content: oven drying at 105–110 °C for 24 h (standard); 60 °C for organic/gypsum soils. Quick methods: sand bath, calcium carbide, alcohol, pycnometer, torsion balance.
Field density: core cutter (soft cohesive soils), sand replacement (gravelly/stony soils), water displacement, rubber balloon, nuclear gauge.

Fig. 2.1 — Three-phase diagram with volume and weight terms and key relations.
Se = wG is the most-used relation; for a fully saturated soil e = wG.
Sieve analysis for coarse fraction (> 75 µm); sedimentation (hydrometer/pipette) for fines (< 75 µm).
Stokes' law: v = (γs − γw)D²/(18μ); valid for 0.2 mm to 0.0002 mm.
Coefficient of uniformity Cu = D60/D10; coefficient of curvature Cc = D30²/(D10·D60).
Well graded: gravel Cu > 4, sand Cu > 6, and Cc = 1–3 for both.
D10 = effective size (Hazen). Uniform soil: Cu ≈ 1. Gap graded: some sizes missing.
States: liquid → LL → plastic → PL → semi-solid → SL → solid.
Liquid limit: water content at which groove (Casagrande device) closes over 13 mm in 25 blows; cone method – 20 mm penetration.
Plastic limit: water content at which soil thread crumbles at 3 mm diameter.
Shrinkage limit: water content below which no further volume reduction on drying (mercury used to find volume).
Plasticity index PI = LL − PL. Shrinkage index = PL − SL.
Liquidity index LI = (w − PL)/PI;  Consistency index CI = (LL − w)/PI;  LI + CI = 1.
LI > 1: soil in liquid state; LI < 0 (CI > 1): semi-solid/very stiff.
Flow index If = slope of flow curve (w vs log N). Toughness index It = PI/If.
Activity A = PI / (% clay < 2 µm): inactive < 0.75; normal 0.75–1.25; active > 1.25. Kaolinite ≈ 0.4, montmorillonite highest.
Sensitivity St = qu (undisturbed) / qu (remoulded, same w): 1 insensitive; 1–2 low; 2–4 medium; 4–8 sensitive; 8–16 extra-sensitive; > 16 quick clay.
Thixotropy: regain of strength with time after remoulding at constant water content.
Free swell index > 50% indicates high swelling (expansive) soil.

Fig. 3.1 — Particle-size distribution curves: well graded, uniformly graded and gap graded soils.
Fig. 3.2 — Atterberg limits on a water-content scale: SL, PL, LL and PI.
Casagrande LL device: Groove closes over 12.7 mm at 25 blows (or cone penetrometer 20 mm in 5 s, 80 g cone).
Toughness index: It = PI / If; Liquidity index LI = 0 at PL, 1 at LL.
Particle sizes (IS): boulder > 300 mm; cobble 80–300; gravel 4.75–80; sand 0.075–4.75; silt 0.002–0.075; clay < 0.002 mm.
Gravel if > 50% of coarse fraction retained on 4.75 mm (No. 4) sieve; otherwise sand.
Symbols: G gravel, S sand, M silt, C clay, O organic, Pt peat, W well graded, P poorly graded, L low, H high plasticity.
USCS: L if LL < 50, H if LL > 50. IS adds I (intermediate): L < 35, I 35–50, H > 50.
Dual symbols (e.g. SW-SM) when fines are 5–12%.
Plasticity chart A-line: PI = 0.73(LL − 20). Above = clays; below = silts and organic soils.
AASHTO (HRB): A-1 to A-7 (A-8 peat); A-1 best subgrade.
Group index GI = 0.2a + 0.005ac + 0.01bd; range 0–20; higher GI = poorer subgrade.
Field identification of fines: dilatancy (shaking), toughness, dry strength. Silt – quick dilatancy, low dry strength; clay – no dilatancy, high dry strength.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 4.1 — Casagrande plasticity chart with A-line and U-line; CL/CI/CH above, ML/MH below.
Plasticity: PI = 24; A-line PI = 0.73(46 − 20) = 19 → above A-line → clay; LL between 35 and 50 → CI (IS) / CL (USCS).
Soils above the A-line are clays (C); below are silts (M) or organic (O). LL 50 separates low (L) from high (H) compressibility.
Basic units: silica tetrahedron; alumina (gibbsite) or magnesia (brucite) octahedron.
Kaolinite: 1:1 layer, strong hydrogen bond; stable, least swelling, low activity.
Illite: 2:1 layer bonded by potassium ions; intermediate behaviour.
Montmorillonite (smectite): 2:1 layer, weak bond with water between layers; maximum swelling, highest specific surface and activity.
Cation replacing power: Li < Na < H < K < NH4 < Mg < Ca < Al.
Adsorbed water / diffuse double layer gives clays plasticity and cohesion.
Structures: single-grained (sands), honeycomb (silts), flocculated (edge-to-face; marine clays, compacted dry of optimum), dispersed (face-to-face; remoulded, compacted wet of optimum).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Montmorillonite: highest swelling, LL, PI, activity and cation exchange capacity; kaolinite: the most stable.
Darcy's law: v = ki (valid for laminar flow, Re < 1). Seepage velocity vs = v/n (vs > v).
Hazen: k = C·D10² (C ≈ 100 with k in cm/s, D10 in cm).
Kozeny–Carman: k ∝ e³/(1+e). k ∝ γw/μ → k increases with temperature.
Factors: grain size, void ratio, viscosity, degree of saturation, soil structure, adsorbed water, entrapped air, organic matter.
Absolute permeability K = kμ/γw (depends only on soil; unit m² or darcy).
Pumping test, confined aquifer (thickness b): k = q·ln(r2/r1) / [2πb(h2 − h1)].
Typical k (cm/s): gravel > 1; clean sand 1–10⁻³; fine sand/silt 10⁻³–10⁻⁵; silty clay 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁷; clay < 10⁻⁷.
Layered soils, flow normal: kv = ΣHi / Σ(Hi/ki). Always kh > kv.
Anisotropic flow net: equivalent k′ = √(kh·kv); transform x by √(kv/kh).

Given: Standpipe a = 1 cm², sample A = 50 cm², L = 10 cm; head falls 50 → 25 cm in 300 s.
Layered deposit: Horizontal permeability always ≥ vertical permeability (kh ≥ kv).
Constant-head test → coarse soils (sands, gravels); falling-head test → fine soils (silts, clays).
Terzaghi: σ = σ′ + u. Strength and compressibility are controlled by effective stress.
Capillary rise hc = 4T cosα/(γw d) ≈ 0.3/d cm (d in cm, pure water). Hazen: hc = C/(e·D10).
In capillary zone pore pressure is negative → effective stress increases.
Upward seepage: σ′ = z(γ′ − iγw). Downward seepage: σ′ = z(γ′ + iγw).
Seepage force per unit volume = iγw (acts in direction of flow).
Critical hydraulic gradient ic = γ′/γw = (G − 1)/(1 + e) ≈ 1.
Quick sand: σ′ = 0 under upward flow at i = ic; a hydraulic condition, not a soil type (fine sands/silts).
Flow net: solution of Laplace equation; flow lines ⟂ equipotentials; elements are curvilinear squares.
Seepage q = kH·(Nf/Nd); Nf/Nd = shape factor.
FS against piping = ic / iexit (3–4 recommended).
Weir/barrage theories: Bligh's creep theory; Lane's weighted creep (horizontal creep weighted 1/3); Khosla's theory.
Earth dam phreatic line: base parabola (Casagrande) with focus at the toe filter; entry correction at upstream face.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Piping & heave: Prevented by cut-offs, longer seepage path, filters, relief wells, weighted filters (inverted filters) at exit.
Quicksand is a hydraulic condition (σ′ = 0), not a type of soil; it happens in fine sands/silts under upward seepage.
Westergaard (stratified soil, thin rigid layers, μ = 0): σz = (Q/πz²)·[1/(1 + 2(r/z)²)]^(3/2); below load 0.3183 Q/z².
Westergaard value ≈ 2/3 of Boussinesq below the load.
Rectangular area: σz = q·I at corner; centre = 4 × corner of quarter rectangle (superposition).
Pressure bulb: zone of significant stress; ≈ 1.5–2B deep for square footings, deeper (≈ 3B or more) for strip footings.
Contact pressure, rigid footing: clay – maximum at edges; sand – maximum at centre.
Flexible footing: uniform pressure; settlement maximum at centre on clay, at edges on sand.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Isobar: Line joining points of equal vertical stress; bulb of 0.2q extends ≈ 1.5B below square footing and ≈ 3B below strip footing.
Compaction: densification by expulsion of air (dynamic, instant). Consolidation: expulsion of water under static load over time.
Standard Proctor: 2.5 kg rammer, 305 mm drop, 3 layers, 25 blows, 1000 cm³ mould; energy ≈ 600 kJ/m³.
Modified Proctor: 4.89 kg rammer, 457 mm drop, 5 layers, 25 blows; energy ≈ 2700 kJ/m³ (≈ 4.5 × standard).
Higher compactive effort → higher γd,max and lower OMC (curve shifts up and left).
Dry of optimum: flocculated structure, higher strength, higher permeability, more swelling, brittle.
Wet of optimum: dispersed structure, lower permeability, more shrinkage, flexible – preferred for earth dam cores.
Well-graded coarse soils: high γd,max, low OMC. Clays: low γd,max, high OMC.
Pneumatic tyred roller: sandy and silty soils, wide range of soils.
Relative compaction RC = γd(field)/γd,max(lab), usually ≥ 95%. Approx. RC = 80 + 0.2 Dr.
Field control: Proctor needle (water content), core cutter, sand replacement.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 9.1 — Compaction curves: standard vs modified Proctor, OMC and zero-air-voids line.
Field density tests: Sand replacement (most common), core cutter (soft cohesive), nuclear density gauge (rapid), balloon method, water displacement.
Specs: Embankments typically ≥ 95% of modified (or standard) Proctor γd,max; subgrade top layers often 98–100%.
More compactive effort → higher γd,max at LOWER OMC; the compaction curve never crosses the zero-air-voids line.
Total settlement = immediate (elastic) + primary consolidation + secondary compression.
Primary: due to expulsion of pore water (dissipation of excess pore pressure). Secondary: creep after excess pore pressure is zero.
Spring analogy explains transfer of load from pore water to soil skeleton.
Terzaghi 1-D assumptions: homogeneous, fully saturated, incompressible solids and water, Darcy's law valid, 1-D flow and compression, k and mv constant, small strains.
Coefficient of compressibility av = −Δe/Δσ′. Coefficient of volume change mv = av/(1 + e0).
Compression index Cc = Δe / log10(σ2′/σ1′) (slope of e–log σ′ line).
Swelling/recompression index Cs ≈ Cc/5 to Cc/10.
OC clay: use Cs up to preconsolidation pressure σp′, then Cc beyond it.
OCR = σp′/σ0′: NC = 1; OC > 1; under-consolidated < 1. σp′ found by Casagrande's graphical method.
Coefficient of consolidation cv = k/(mv·γw). Time factor Tv = cv·t/d².
Drainage path d = H/2 (double drainage), H (single drainage). t ∝ d² → double drainage is 4 times faster.
Oedometer: fixed or floating ring; load increment ratio 1; each load ≈ 24 h.
Secondary compression index Cα = Δe/Δlog t; Ss = [Cα·H/(1 + ep)]·log(t2/t1).
Excess pore pressure is maximum at mid-depth (double drainage) or at the impervious boundary (single drainage).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 10.1 — e–log σ′ curve: recompression, preconsolidation pressure, virgin compression (Cc) and swelling (Cs).
Given: NC clay 4 m thick, e₀ = 1.0, Cc = 0.30, σ₀′ = 80 kPa at mid-depth, Δσ = 40 kPa.
Time (double drainage): d = 2 m; for U = 90%, t = 0.848 d²/cv.
Time for given U ∝ d² — doubling drainage path quadruples consolidation time; single drainage takes 4× longer than double for the same layer.

s.t: More on this topic — Foundation Engineering & Advanced Soil Mechanics: Advanced Consolidation & Secondary Compression
b: Terzaghi 1-D theory: ∂u/∂t = cv ∂²u/∂z²; Tv = cv t / Hdr²; Tv(50%) = 0.197, Tv(90%) = 0.848; Tv = (π/4)U² for U < 60%.
Lab-to-field time: t_field/t_lab = (Hdr,field/Hdr,lab)² (same U). Example: 20 mm sample (double drainage, Hdr = 10 mm) 50% in 10 min → 5 m single drainage layer: 10 × (5000/10)² min ≈ 4.75 years.
Determining cv: Casagrande log-time (t50) and Taylor root-time (t90) fitting methods.
Pre-consolidation pressure: Casagrande construction on e–log σ′ curve; OCR = σ′p/σ′₀.
Settlement equations: NC: Sc = Cc H/(1 + e₀) log(σ′f/σ′₀); OC with σ′f ≤ σ′p: use Cs.
Secondary compression: Ss = Cα H log(t₂/t₁)/(1 + ep); significant in organic soils/peat.
Acceleration: Preloading/surcharge + vertical (sand/PVD) drains — radial consolidation (Barron); drain spacing controls time.
Double drainage halves Hdr → time reduces to one quarter for the same degree of consolidation.
Mohr–Coulomb: τf = c + σ tanφ; effective: τf = c′ + σ′ tanφ′.
Failure plane inclined at 45° + φ/2 to the major principal plane.
Maximum shear stress acts on a 45° plane, but failure plane coincides with it only when φ = 0.
Direct shear test: failure plane predetermined, non-uniform stress, poor drainage control, no pore pressure measurement.
Triaxial test: drainage controlled, pore pressure measured; types UU, CU, CD.
UU: φu = 0 for saturated clay. CU: gives total and effective parameters. CD: slow test, gives c′, φ′.
Unconfined compression: special triaxial with σ3 = 0; for clays cu = qu/2.
Vane shear: in-situ undrained strength of soft/sensitive clays. T = πD²c(H/2 + D/6) (both ends shearing).
UU applications: end-of-construction of embankments/footings on saturated clay.
Sands: c = 0, φ ≈ 28–45°. Dense sand shows peak strength and dilation; loose sand contracts.
Critical void ratio: void ratio at which shearing causes no volume change.
Liquefaction: loose saturated fine sand under cyclic (earthquake) loading; pore pressure rises, σ′ → 0.
Skempton: Δu = B[Δσ3 + A(Δσ1 − Δσ3)]. B = 1 saturated, 0 dry.
Af: NC clay 0.5–1; heavily OC clay negative; sensitive clay > 1.
NC clay: c′ ≈ 0. Residual strength used for long-term stability of old slip surfaces.
Stress path: p = (σ1 + σ3)/2, q = (σ1 − σ3)/2. Kf line: tanα = sinφ; intercept a = c·cosφ.

s.t: More on this topic — Foundation Engineering & Advanced Soil Mechanics: Advanced Shear Strength — Triaxial, Pore Pressure & Stress Paths
b: Triaxial tests: UU (quick, total stress, φu = 0 for saturated clay), CU (with pore-pressure measurement → c′, φ′), CD (slow, drained — sands, long term).
Back pressure: Applied to saturate the specimen (dissolve air) — check by Skempton B ≥ 0.95 (CE-335 question).
Skempton pore-pressure parameters: Δu = B[Δσ₃ + A(Δσ₁ − Δσ₃)]; B = 1 for saturated soil; Af ≈ 1 (NC clay), ≈ 0 to −0.5 (heavily OC clay).
Dense vs loose sand (direct shear): Dense: peak then softening, dilation (volume increase); loose: no peak, contraction; both reach the same critical (constant-volume) state.
Stress paths: MIT: p = (σ₁ + σ₃)/2, q = (σ₁ − σ₃)/2; Cambridge: p′ = (σ′₁ + 2σ′₃)/3, q = σ′₁ − σ′₃. Kf-line: a = c cos φ, tan α = sin φ.
Sensitivity & thixotropy: St = qu(undisturbed)/qu(remoulded); quick clays St > 16; thixotropy = regain of strength with time.
For a CD test with σ₃ = 100 and deviator 250 kPa: σ₁ = 350; sin φ′ = (350 − 100)/(350 + 100) → φ′ ≈ 33.7°.
Fig. 12.1 — Critical state line, yield surfaces and NCL in q–p′ and e–ln p′ spaces.
Critical state: Soil sheared continuously at constant volume, constant stresses: q = M p′ and e = eΓ − λ ln p′.
M: Triaxial compression M = 6 sin φ′cs / (3 − sin φ′cs).
Normal consolidation line: e = eN − λ ln p′; unloading–reloading lines slope κ (Cc ≈ 2.3λ, Cs ≈ 2.3κ).
Wet vs dry side: Lightly OC (wet of critical): contract, positive pore pressure, hardening. Heavily OC (dry of critical): dilate, negative pore pressure, peak then softening.
Cam-Clay models: Original & Modified Cam Clay (elliptical yield surface) — basis of advanced FE soil models.
Critical-state friction angle is a material constant independent of initial density.
At rest (no wall movement): Jaky K0 = 1 − sinφ′ (NC). Elastic: K0 = μ/(1 − μ). OC: K0 = (1 − sinφ′)·OCR^sinφ′.
Active (wall moves away from soil) < at rest < passive (wall moves towards soil).
Passive state needs much larger wall movement than active.
Rankine (smooth vertical wall, horizontal backfill): Ka = (1 − sinφ)/(1 + sinφ) = tan²(45° − φ/2); Kp = 1/Ka.
Active failure plane at 45° + φ/2 to horizontal; passive at 45° − φ/2.
Active thrust Pa = ½ Ka γ H², acting at H/3 above base.
Surcharge q: uniform pressure Ka·q; resultant acts at H/2.
Submerged backfill: p = Ka γ′ z + γw z.
Depth of tension crack zc = 2c/(γ√Ka); for φ = 0, zc = 2c/γ.
Critical height of unsupported vertical cut Hc = 4c/(γ√Ka); φ = 0: Hc = 4c/γ.
Coulomb wedge theory: includes wall friction δ, inclined wall, sloping backfill; plane failure surface.
Coulomb overestimates passive pressure (actual surface curved). Graphical methods: Rebhann, Culmann.
Rankine ignores wall friction → conservative (higher) active pressure.
Retaining wall checks: overturning (FS ≥ 1.5–2), sliding (FS ≥ 1.5), bearing pressure, no tension (e ≤ B/6).
Provide weep holes/drainage to avoid water pressure behind the wall.
Anchored sheet piles: free earth support and fixed earth support methods. Braced cuts: Peck's apparent pressure diagrams.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 13.1 — Rankine active and passive earth pressure: wall movement, failure planes and triangular pressure.
Given: Wall 6 m high, dry sand γ = 18 kN/m³, φ = 30°.
Thrust: Pa = ½ × ⅓ × 18 × 6² = 108 kN/m, acting 2 m above the base.
With water table at surface: p = Ka γ′ z + γw z → water pressure often exceeds the soil pressure — hence weep holes and drainage.
Movement needed: active ≈ 0.1–0.5% of H (small); passive ≈ 2–5% of H (large).

s.t: More on this topic — Foundation Engineering & Advanced Soil Mechanics: Retaining Walls — Stability Design
b: Types: Gravity, semi-gravity, cantilever (economical up to ≈ 6–7 m), counterfort (> 7 m), buttressed, crib, gabion, MSE (reinforced earth), anchored.
Earth pressure at rest: K₀ = 1 − sin φ′ (Jaky) — wall restrained against yielding (CE-335 question).
Rankine: Ka = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ); Kp = 1/Ka; Pa = ½ Ka γ H² at H/3; cohesive soil tension depth zc = 2c/(γ√Ka).
Water table in backfill: Undrained backfill: use γ′ below WT + full hydrostatic pressure; thrust much larger → provide weep holes & drains.
Coulomb: Considers wall friction δ and inclined back/backfill; gives smaller Ka than Rankine for δ > 0.
Stability checks: Overturning FS ≥ 2.0; sliding FS ≥ 1.5; bearing (qmax ≤ qa) with e ≤ B/6; overall (deep-seated) stability FS ≥ 1.5.
Proportioning (cantilever): Base width ≈ 0.5–0.7 H; toe ≈ B/3; stem top ≥ 200–300 mm; base thickness ≈ H/10–H/12; shear key to improve sliding resistance.
Passive pressure in front of the toe is often ignored in sliding checks (soil may be removed).
Cantilever sheet piles: Rely on passive resistance below dredge line; economical up to ≈ 6 m retained height.
Anchored sheet piles: Free-earth support method (shallower, anchor carries more) vs fixed-earth support (deeper embedment); Rowe's moment reduction for flexibility.
Braced cuts: Peck's apparent pressure diagrams: sand 0.65 Ka γ H (uniform); soft–medium clay γH − 4cu (or 0.3γH min) trapezoid; stiff clay 0.2–0.4 γH.
Base heave (soft clay): FS = cu Nc / (γH + q) (Bjerrum–Eide); stability number N = γH/cu > 6–8 indicates heave risk.
Dewatering: Well points (≤ 5–6 m lift per stage), deep wells, electro-osmosis for silts.
Strut loads in braced cuts are found from apparent pressure envelopes, not Rankine triangles.
Infinite slope, dry cohesionless: FS = tanφ/tanβ; stable up to β = φ (angle of repose). Same for fully submerged.
Infinite slope with seepage parallel to slope: FS = (γ′/γsat)·tanφ/tanβ ≈ ½ of dry value.
Infinite slope, c–φ soil: critical depth Hc = c / [γ cos²β (tanβ − tanφ)].
Swedish circle / ordinary method of slices (Fellenius): ignores interslice forces; conservative.
Bishop's simplified method: includes horizontal interslice forces; more accurate; iterative.
Friction circle method (Taylor) for c–φ soils.
Taylor's stability number Sn = c/(F·γ·H); critical height Hc = c/(Sn·γ).
Failure circles: toe, slope (face) and base failure (soft layer below toe).
FS defined w.r.t. cohesion (Fc), friction (Fφ) and height (FH). Usual minimum FS ≈ 1.5.
Earth dam critical cases: upstream slope – sudden drawdown; downstream slope – steady seepage (reservoir full); both – end of construction.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 15.1 — Slip circles: toe, slope (face) and base failure.
Typical FS required: Long-term slopes ≈ 1.5; end-of-construction ≈ 1.3; rapid drawdown ≈ 1.2–1.3; seismic ≈ 1.0–1.1.
Landslides in Pakistan: Frequent along KKH, Murree–Kohala, Swat & Kohistan roads; remedies — drainage (horizontal drains), retaining/breast walls, rock bolting, slope flattening, bio-engineering.
Infinite slope in dry sand: FS = tanφ/tanβ (independent of depth); with steady seepage parallel to slope, FS ≈ halved.
Gross ultimate qu; net ultimate qnu = qu − γDf; net safe qns = qnu/F; safe qs = qnu/F + γDf. F usually 2.5–3.
Allowable bearing pressure = lesser of safe bearing capacity and pressure for permissible settlement.
Skempton (clay): Nc = 5.14 strip, 6.2 square/circle at surface; increases with Df/B up to 7.5 (strip) and 9 (square).
General shear failure: dense sand, stiff clay; well-defined surface, heaving, tilting.
Local shear: medium soils; Terzaghi uses c′ = (2/3)c, tanφ′ = (2/3)tanφ.
Punching shear: loose sand, soft clay, deep footings; no heave.
Water table at base of footing: Nγ term reduced (≈ half). At ground surface: both γ terms reduced → large loss of capacity.
Clay (φ = 0): bearing capacity independent of width B. Sand: increases with B and Df.
Meyerhof, Hansen, Vesic, IS 6403: add shape, depth and inclination factors.
Eccentric load: q = (P/A)(1 ± 6e/B); no tension if e ≤ B/6 (middle third). Meyerhof effective width B′ = B − 2e.
Permissible settlement (Terzaghi–Peck): 25 mm for footings on sand. Angular distortion 1/500 safe limit for buildings (Bjerrum).
Plate load test: plate ≥ 300 mm; pit width ≥ 5 × plate width.
Plate test, sand: qf = qp(Bf/Bp); Sf = Sp·[Bf(Bp + 0.3)/(Bp(Bf + 0.3))]² (B in m).
Plate test limitations: short duration, size effect, influence depth only ≈ 2 × plate width.

Strap (cantilever) footing: Exterior footing connected by a rigid strap beam to an interior footing; strap transfers moment, does not bear on soil.
Mat / raft: When footings cover > 50% of building area, weak soil, or to reduce differential settlement; types: flat plate, thickened under columns, beam-and-slab, cellular, piled raft.
Compensated (floating) foundation: Net pressure qnet = Q/A − γDf → zero when excavated soil weight = building load (fully compensated).
Analysis: Rigid (conventional) method vs flexible (Winkler / modulus of subgrade reaction ks; beam on elastic foundation, FEM).

Piles used for: weak upper strata, heavy loads, uplift, lateral loads, scour, expansive soils.
By function: end bearing, friction, compaction, tension (uplift), anchor, fender, batter, sheet piles.

Clay group: check block failure Qg = cNc·Ab + c·P·L (Nc = 9). Sand (driven): η may exceed 1.

Well foundation parts: cutting edge, curb, steining, bottom plug, sand filling, top plug, well cap.
Well shapes: circular, dumb-bell, double-D, rectangular. Grip length ≥ 1/3 of maximum scour depth.
Permissible well tilt 1 in 80; shift 150 mm.

Classification: By function: end-bearing, friction, compaction, tension (uplift), anchor, batter (inclined loads), sheet. By material/installation: driven (displacement) vs bored/cast-in-situ (non-displacement).
Static capacity: Qu = Qb + Qs = qb Ab + Σ fs As. Clay: qb = 9 cu; fs = α cu (α-method), β-method fs = β σ′v, λ-method. Sand: qb = σ′v Nq* (limited), fs = K σ′v tan δ.
Critical depth (sand): Skin friction & end bearing assumed constant below ≈ 15–20 D (Meyerhof/Vesic).
Dynamic formulas: Engineering News: Qa = W h / (6(s + c)) (c = 25 mm drop hammer, 2.5 mm steam); Hiley formula; wave-equation & PDA for modern practice.
Pile groups: Group efficiency (Converse–Labarre) η = 1 − θ[(n−1)m + (m−1)n]/(90mn), θ = tan⁻¹(d/s); clay block failure: Qg = 9cu·B·L + 2(B + L)·Lp·c̄.
Negative skin friction: Downdrag when surrounding soil settles relative to pile (fill over soft clay, lowering WT); Qn = perimeter × length × α cu.

Load tests: Maintained load test; failure load: settlement = 10% of D or double-tangent; allowable (IS 2911) = lesser of ⅔ of the load at 12 mm settlement and ½ of the load at settlement = 10% of D; cyclic test separates skin & tip.
Wells/caissons: Open, box, pneumatic caissons; well foundations for bridge piers in rivers (grip length ≥ ⅓ of maximum scour depth).
Pile group in clay: capacity = smaller of (n × single pile) and block failure. Negative skin friction reduces allowable capacity.
Methods: test pits (shallow), auger boring, wash boring (disturbed samples), percussion drilling (boulders), rotary drilling (rock).
Depth of exploration: till stress increase becomes negligible (≈ 10% of applied); ≈ 1.5–2B for isolated footings.
Area ratio Ar = (Do² − Di²)/Di² × 100; ≤ 10% for undisturbed sampling (thin-walled).
Inside clearance 1–3% (reduces wall friction); outside clearance 0–2%.
Recovery ratio = length of sample / penetration (≈ 0.96–0.98 good).
Samplers: split spoon (disturbed, SPT), Shelby/thin-walled tube (soft clays), piston sampler (very soft/sensitive clays), Denison (stiff clays), core barrels (rock).
RQD = Σ core pieces ≥ 100 mm / length of run × 100: < 25 very poor; 25–50 poor; 50–75 fair; 75–90 good; 90–100 excellent.
SPT: 63.5 kg hammer, 750 mm drop, split spoon 50.8 mm OD; N = blows for last 300 mm of 450 mm penetration.
SPT corrections: overburden, energy (N60), dilatancy N′ = 15 + ½(N − 15) for N > 15 in fine/silty sand below WT.
N (sand): 0–4 very loose; 4–10 loose; 10–30 medium; 30–50 dense; > 50 very dense.
Static cone (CPT): 60° cone, 10 cm² base, pushed at 2 cm/s; cone resistance qc and friction ratio identify soil type.
Dynamic cone test: continuous record of blows; quick, approximate.
Seismic refraction: works only if wave velocity increases with depth.
Electrical resistivity (Wenner array, 4 equally spaced electrodes): ρ = 2πaR.
Groundwater table recorded at least 24 h after boring.

Number of boreholes: ≈ one per 200–400 m² for buildings (at least 3); at 30–50 m along roads/pipelines.
Rock quality: RQD: < 25% very poor; 25–50 poor; 50–75 fair; 75–90 good; 90–100 excellent.
Undisturbed samples need area ratio ≤ 10% (thin-walled Shelby tubes); split spoon (SPT) gives disturbed samples.

Direct methods: test pits, trenches, shafts, adits, borings.
Boring types: auger, wash, percussion, rotary; core drilling (diamond bit) for rock samples.

Electrical resistivity (Wenner, Schlumberger arrays): groundwater, clay layers, depth to rock. Dry rock = high resistivity; saline water/clay = low.
Gravity & magnetic: cavities, ore bodies, buried structures. GPR: shallow utilities, voids.
Geophysical results must be confirmed by boreholes.

GSI (Hoek): based on structure and surface condition of joints.
Other tests: UCS, point load index, slake durability (shale), Schmidt hammer.

Typical CBR values: Clay ≈ 2–5%; silt ≈ 5–10%; sand ≈ 10–40%; gravel ≈ 30–80%; crushed stone base ≥ 80%.
CBR = test load ÷ standard load × 100 at 2.5 mm (1370 kg) and 5.0 mm (2055 kg) penetration; plunger area 19.6 cm² (50 mm dia).
Expansive soils: montmorillonite; remedies – under-reamed piles, CNS (cohesive non-swelling) layer, sand cushion, lime stabilization, moisture control.
Collapsible soils (loess): sudden settlement on wetting; remedy – prewetting, compaction, chemical stabilization.
Cement stabilization: best for sandy/granular soils. Lime: clayey soils (reduces PI, swelling).
Bitumen: waterproofing/binding granular soils. Chemicals: CaCl2, NaCl, sodium silicate.
Electro-osmosis: drainage of silts and clays. Thermal: heating/freezing.
Vibroflotation: densifying deep loose sands. Stone columns: soft clays.
Sand drains / prefabricated vertical (wick) drains: accelerate consolidation by radial drainage (Barron); smear zone reduces efficiency.
Grouting: cement, chemical, jet grouting. Dewatering: well points, deep wells.
Reinforced earth (Henri Vidal), soil nailing, geosynthetics.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Lime stabilisation: Best for clays (reduces PI, swelling); cement for sandy/granular soils; bitumen for sands (waterproofing).
Geosynthetics: Geotextiles (separation, filtration, drainage), geogrids (reinforcement), geomembranes (barrier, landfills/canal lining), geocells, GCLs.
Stone columns: Vibro-replacement columns in soft clays — reinforcement + faster drainage.
Vibroflotation densifies loose SANDS; sand drains/PVDs + preloading accelerate consolidation of soft CLAYS.
Liquefaction: Loss of strength of loose, saturated, clean/silty sands under cyclic loading as pore pressure rises to σ′v (effective stress → 0).
Susceptibility: Loose (N₁,60 < 15–20), saturated, uniformly graded fine sands, shallow WT, strong shaking (M > 5.5).
Evaluation: Seed–Idriss simplified: CSR = 0.65 (amax/g)(σv/σ′v) rd vs CRR from SPT/CPT/Vs; FS = CRR/CSR.
Mitigation: Densification (vibro-compaction, dynamic compaction), stone columns (drainage), grouting, deep soil mixing, piles to non-liquefiable layer.
Machine foundations: Avoid resonance: operating frequency should differ from natural frequency by ≥ 20–30%; block foundation mass ≈ 2–3 × machine mass.
Liquefaction is most likely in loose saturated fine sand with high water table during strong earthquakes.
75 µm sieve divides coarse and fine soils; 4.75 mm divides gravel and sand.
A-line PI = 0.73(LL − 20); LL 50 divides L and H (USCS).
Terzaghi Nc (φ = 0) = 5.7; Skempton strip = 5.14; pile end bearing Nc = 9.

Geology: science of the Earth – its materials, structure and processes.
Engineering geology: application of geology to the location, design, construction and maintenance of civil works.
Age of Earth: ≈ 4.54 billion years. Mean radius: ≈ 6371 km.
Crust: oceanic 5–10 km (basaltic, SIMA = Si + Mg); continental 30–70 km (granitic, SIAL = Si + Al).
Mantle: Moho to ≈ 2900 km. Gutenberg discontinuity: mantle–core boundary (2900 km).
Outer core: liquid (2900–5150 km) – proved because S-waves do not pass through it.
Inner core: solid Fe–Ni (5150–6371 km). Lehmann discontinuity: outer–inner core boundary.
Lithosphere: crust + upper rigid mantle (≈ 100 km); rests on the plastic asthenosphere.
Abundant elements in crust: O (46.6%) > Si (27.7%) > Al (8.1%) > Fe (5%) > Ca > Na > K > Mg.
Abundant minerals: silicates ≈ 90% of crust; feldspars are the most abundant group.
Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian, Devonian, Carboniferous, Permian
Age of mammals; Himalaya uplift; humans (Quaternary)
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 26.1 — Internal structure of the Earth and its discontinuities.
Moho (crust–mantle), Gutenberg (mantle–core; S-waves disappear), Lehmann (outer–inner core). Outer core is liquid.
Mineral: naturally occurring, inorganic, solid with definite chemical composition and crystal structure.
Physical properties: colour, streak (colour of powder – more reliable than colour), lustre, hardness, cleavage, fracture, specific gravity, crystal form.
Cleavage: breaking along definite planes; fracture: irregular breaking (quartz shows conchoidal fracture).
Quartz (SiO₂) – H 7, no cleavage, most resistant to weathering.
Calcite (CaCO₃) – H 3, effervesces with cold dilute HCl. Dolomite CaMg(CO₃)₂ reacts only with warm/powdered HCl.
Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) – H 2; harmful in foundations (soluble, swelling). Mica – perfect cleavage in one direction.
Clay minerals: kaolinite (least swelling), illite, montmorillonite (highest swelling – expansive soils).
Field tests: fingernail ≈ 2.5, copper coin ≈ 3.5, knife / glass ≈ 5.5. Scale is relative, not linear.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fingernail ≈ 2.5, copper coin ≈ 3, knife/glass ≈ 5.5; quartz (7) scratches glass.
Intrusive / plutonic: cool slowly at depth → coarse grained (granite, diorite, gabbro).
Extrusive / volcanic: cool fast at surface → fine grained / glassy (rhyolite, andesite, basalt, obsidian, pumice).
By silica: acid > 66% (granite), intermediate 52–66% (diorite), basic 45–52% (basalt, gabbro), ultrabasic < 45% (peridotite).
Intrusive forms: dyke (discordant, vertical), sill (concordant, horizontal), batholith (largest), laccolith (dome), lopolith (saucer), phacolith (in fold crests/troughs).
Granite: high strength, good foundation and building stone; basalt: strong, used as aggregate, may show columnar joints.
Cover ≈ 75% of Earth’s land surface but only ≈ 5% of crust volume.
Clastic: conglomerate (rounded gravel), breccia (angular fragments), sandstone, siltstone, shale (most abundant sedimentary rock).
Chemical: limestone, rock salt, gypsum. Organic: coal, chalk, coquina.
Features: stratification (bedding), fossils, ripple marks, mud cracks, cross-bedding.
Sandstone strength depends on cement: siliceous (best) > ferruginous > calcareous > argillaceous (weakest).
Shale: weak, slakes and swells with water – poor for dams/tunnels. Limestone: solution cavities (karst) → leakage, sinkholes.

s.t: Metamorphic Rocks (change by heat, pressure, fluids)
b: Contact (thermal): heat near intrusion – non-foliated. Regional (dynamothermal): heat + pressure over large area – foliated.
Rock cycle: igneous ⇄ sedimentary ⇄ metamorphic through weathering, deposition, metamorphism and melting.
Strike: direction of line formed by intersection of bed with a horizontal plane.
Dip: maximum inclination of bed from horizontal; measured perpendicular to strike. Apparent dip < true dip.
Outcrop: exposure of rock at surface. Inlier: older rocks surrounded by younger. Outlier: younger rocks surrounded by older.
Parts: hinge, limbs, axial plane, crest, trough, plunge.
Anticline: up-arched, oldest beds at core. Syncline: down-folded, youngest beds at core.
Other types: monocline (one-limbed step), symmetrical, asymmetrical, overturned, recumbent (axial plane ~horizontal), isoclinal (parallel limbs), chevron, plunging, dome, basin.
Combination of dip and strike slip
Horst: up-thrown block between two normal faults; graben: down-dropped block (rift valley).
Evidence: slickensides, fault breccia, fault gouge, offset beds, springs in a line, scarps.
Faults are zones of weakness and seepage → avoid for dams, tunnels and heavy structures; active faults cause earthquakes.
Joint: fracture with no displacement – tension, shear, columnar (basalt), sheet joints (granite).
Unconformity: surface of erosion/non-deposition (time gap) in the rock record.
Angular unconformity: younger beds over tilted/folded older beds.
Paraconformity: parallel beds, gap hard to detect.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 29.1 — Normal, reverse (thrust) and strike-slip faults.
Strike & dip: Strike = direction of a horizontal line on the bed; dip = maximum inclination, measured ⊥ to strike (clinometer/Brunton compass).
Normal fault → tension (hanging wall down); reverse/thrust → compression (hanging wall up); strike-slip → horizontal shear (Chaman fault, Pakistan–Afghanistan).
Porosity (n) = Vv / V; permeability = ability to transmit water.

Aquifer: porous and permeable (sand, gravel, jointed rock). Aquiclude: porous but impermeable (clay). Aquitard: poorly permeable, leaky (silt, sandy clay). Aquifuge: neither porous nor permeable (massive granite).
Unconfined aquifer: upper surface is water table. Confined / artesian: between impermeable layers, water under pressure (flowing well if piezometric surface above ground).
Perched water table: local water body above main water table on a lens of clay.
Pumping produces a cone of depression. Springs occur where water table meets ground surface.
Groundwater effects: uplift, reduced effective stress, slope failure, tunnel inflow, liquefaction potential.

chapters.t: Geology of Dams, Reservoirs, Tunnels & Slopes

b: Ideal site: narrow valley, sound impervious bedrock at shallow depth, no active faults, low seismicity, construction material nearby.
Gravity dam: needs strong rock foundation. Arch dam: narrow V-shaped gorge with strong abutments. Earth/rockfill dam: can be built on weaker foundations.
Beds dipping upstream (steeply) = favourable. Beds dipping downstream = sliding and leakage risk.
Avoid: faults/shear zones, cavernous limestone, soluble gypsum, swelling shale, highly jointed rock.
Treatments: curtain grouting (reduce seepage), consolidation grouting (strengthen rock), cut-off walls/trenches, drainage galleries, relief wells.
Must be watertight, with stable rim slopes and low sediment inflow.
Problems: leakage through limestone/faults, siltation, rim landslides (e.g. Vajont 1963, Italy), reservoir-induced seismicity (e.g. Koyna 1967, India).
Best in massive, hard, unjointed rock; tunnel axis preferably perpendicular to strike.
Tunnel along a syncline axis → water inflow and high pressure; along an anticline axis → beds arch, less load but crown rock is fractured.

Problems: overbreak, squeezing ground (plastic soft rock), swelling ground (montmorillonite, anhydrite), running ground (loose sand), rock burst (hard brittle rock at great depth), groundwater, gases, high temperature.
Support: rock bolts, shotcrete, wire mesh, steel ribs, lining; NATM (New Austrian Tunnelling Method) uses rock as part of support.
Types (Varnes): falls, topples, slides (rotational / slump; translational / planar), spreads, flows (debris flow, mudflow, earthflow), creep (slowest – tilted poles, trees).
Main trigger: water (rise in pore pressure). Others: undercutting of toe, slope steepening, earthquakes, deforestation, loading of crest.
Control: drainage (most effective & economical), slope flattening/benching, retaining walls, gabions, rock bolts/anchors, toe berms, vegetation.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Pakistan examples: Tarbela (Indus) on alluvium with huge upstream blanket against seepage; Mangla on sandstone–clay (Siwalik) rocks; tunnels in KKH region face squeezing ground and rock bursts.
Best dam site rock: massive, unweathered igneous rock (granite); worst: cavernous limestone, highly jointed or soluble rocks (gypsum).
Continental drift: Alfred Wegener (1912); supercontinent Pangaea, ocean Panthalassa; split into Laurasia (N) and Gondwana (S).
Sea-floor spreading: Harry Hess (1960s). Plate tectonics unified both theories.
Driving force: mantle convection, slab pull, ridge push.
Divergent boundary: plates move apart – mid-ocean ridge, rift valley (East African Rift).

Convergent boundary: plates collide – oceanic–continental (subduction, trench, volcanic arc e.g. Andes), oceanic–oceanic (island arcs, Japan), continental–continental (Himalaya, Indian–Eurasian plates).
Transform boundary: plates slide past – San Andreas Fault (USA), Chaman Fault (Pakistan–Afghanistan).
Indian plate moves north at ≈ 4–5 cm/year.
Main Karakoram Thrust (MKT), Main Mantle Thrust (MMT), Main Boundary Thrust (MBT), Salt Range Thrust – northern collision zone.
Chaman Fault – left-lateral (sinistral) transform fault, western boundary of Indian plate.
Makran Subduction Zone – Arabian plate subducting under Eurasian plate (tsunami source).
Earthquake: sudden shaking of ground due to release of strain energy in the Earth.
Causes: tectonic (most common), volcanic, collapse (caves/mines), induced (reservoirs, mining, fluid injection, explosions).
Elastic rebound theory: H.F. Reid, after 1906 San Francisco earthquake – rocks store strain and snap back on rupture.
Focus / hypocentre: point of origin inside Earth. Epicentre: point on surface vertically above focus.
Focal depth: shallow < 70 km (most damaging, most common), intermediate 70–300 km, deep 300–700 km.
Seismic belts: Circum-Pacific “Ring of Fire” (≈ 80% of earthquakes), Alpide / Mediterranean–Himalayan belt (≈ 15–17%, includes Pakistan), mid-oceanic ridges.
Wadati–Benioff zone: inclined zone of earthquakes along a subducting slab.
Fastest (≈ 5–8 km/s in crust); arrives first
≈ 3–4.5 km/s; absent through outer core → liquid core
Body waves = P & S; surface waves = Love & Rayleigh (cause most damage).
Order of arrival: P → S → Love → Rayleigh.
Shadow zones: S-wave shadow 103°–180° from epicentre; P-wave shadow 103°–142°.
Locating epicentre: S–P time interval gives distance (roughly ≈ 8 km per second of S–P lag); minimum 3 stations needed (triangulation).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 34.1 — Particle motion of P, S, Love and Rayleigh waves.
Order of arrival: P → S → Love → Rayleigh. S–P time difference gives the distance to the epicentre (≈ 8 km per second of S–P lag).
Seismograph / seismometer: records ground motion; record = seismogram. Accelerograph: records strong-motion acceleration (used in design).
Magnitude: measure of energy released – one value per earthquake, instrumental.
Intensity: measure of effects/damage at a place – varies with distance, soil and construction; observational.
Richter scale (ML): Charles Richter, 1935, logarithmic; open-ended (no upper limit).
One unit increase in magnitude = 10× amplitude and ≈ 32× energy (two units ≈ 1000× energy).
Other magnitudes: mb (body wave), Ms (surface wave), Mw (moment magnitude) – Hanks & Kanamori 1979; does not saturate for large events.
Seismic moment: M₀ = μ·A·D (rigidity × fault area × average slip). Mw = (2/3)(log₁₀ M₀ − 9.1), M₀ in N·m.
Intensity scales: Modified Mercalli (MMI, I–XII, Roman numerals), MSK-64, EMS-98, JMA (0–7).
Isoseismal lines: lines joining points of equal intensity. Peak ground acceleration (PGA): expressed as fraction of g.
Largest recorded earthquake: 1960 Valdivia, Chile – Mw 9.5.
Ground shaking (main cause of damage), surface fault rupture, landslides, fires, dam failure.

Liquefaction: loose, saturated, fine/uniform sand loses strength as pore pressure rises and effective stress → 0. Signs: sand boils, tilting/sinking buildings (Niigata, Japan 1964). Susceptible: low SPT N, shallow water table, young deposits.
Remedies for liquefaction: densification (vibro-compaction, dynamic compaction), stone columns, drains, grouting, deep foundations.
Site amplification: soft soil deposits amplify shaking (Mexico City 1985).
Resonance: damage peaks when natural period of building ≈ period of ground motion. Natural period roughly ≈ 0.1 × number of storeys (s).

Tsunami (Japanese: “harbour wave”): caused by vertical sea-floor displacement in undersea earthquakes; very long wavelength, speed ≈ √(g·d). Examples: 2004 Indian Ocean (Mw 9.1), 2011 Tohoku (Mw 9.0), 1945 Makran (hit Pasni).
Seiche: oscillation of water in enclosed basins (lakes, reservoirs).

Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Major Pakistani earthquakes: 1935 Quetta (Mw ≈ 7.7, ≈ 30,000+ deaths); 1945 Makran (Mw 8.1, tsunami); 1974 Pattan; 2005 Kashmir (Mw 7.6, ≈ 86,000 deaths); 2013 Awaran (Mw 7.7); 2015 Hindu Kush (Mw 7.5).
Tectonic setting: Indian plate colliding with Eurasian plate in the north (Himalaya–Karakoram–Hindu Kush); transform boundary along Chaman fault in the west; Makran subduction zone in the south-west.
BCP seismic zones run from Zone 1 (lowest) to Zone 4 (highest); Islamabad/Peshawar areas are in Zone 2B–3; Quetta and northern areas in Zone 3–4.
Keep building light, simple, symmetric and regular in plan and elevation; provide a continuous load path.
Avoid: soft storey (open ground floor), short columns, plan irregularity (L, T shapes → torsion), re-entrant corners, heavy overhangs, abrupt stiffness/mass changes.
Provide seismic gap / separation joints between adjacent blocks to prevent pounding.
Ductility: ability to deform inelastically without collapse – key to absorbing seismic energy.
Strong column – weak beam philosophy: plastic hinges form in beams, not columns.
Design philosophy: no damage in minor, repairable damage in moderate, no collapse in major earthquakes (life safety).
Moment-resisting frames (OMRF, IMRF, SMRF), shear walls, braced frames (concentric, eccentric), dual systems.
Base isolation: lead–rubber bearings, friction pendulum – lengthen period, reduce forces.
Energy dissipation: viscous, friction, yielding dampers; tuned mass damper (e.g. Taipei 101).
Closely spaced ties/stirrups near beam–column joints and column ends (confinement zone).
Ties with 135° seismic hooks; no lap splices in plastic hinge zones.
Horizontal RC bands: plinth, sill, lintel (most important), roof bands.
Vertical reinforcement at corners and junctions; limit size and number of openings; avoid openings near corners.
Use good-quality mortar and through-stones; light roofs tied to walls.
Design base shear: V = (Cv · I / R · T) · W
Upper limit: V ≤ 2.5 · Ca · I · W / R
Lower limit: V ≥ 0.11 · Ca · I · W
Cv, Ca = seismic coefficients (zone + soil profile); I = importance factor; R = response modification factor; W = seismic weight; T = fundamental period.
Fundamental period: T = Ct · (hn)^¾ ; Ct = 0.0853 (steel MRF), 0.0731 (RC MRF), 0.0488 (other) with hn in metres.
Base shear distributed over height as storey forces; part applied at top as Ft = 0.07·T·V (when T > 0.7 s).
Analysis methods: equivalent static (seismic coefficient), response spectrum (dynamic), time-history (most accurate).
Response spectrum: plot of peak response (acceleration/velocity/displacement) of SDOF systems vs natural period for a given damping (usually 5%).
Mineral that fizzes with cold dilute HCl – calcite.
Most abundant mineral group – feldspar; most resistant to weathering – quartz.
Granite is intrusive, acidic; basalt is extrusive, basic.
Marble from limestone; quartzite from sandstone; slate from shale; gneiss from granite.
Oldest beds in core – anticline; youngest in core – syncline.
Hanging wall moves down – normal fault (tension); up – reverse/thrust (compression).
Clay is an aquiclude; massive granite is an aquifuge.
Best rock for dam foundation – massive igneous (granite); worst – cavernous limestone, shale, gypsum.
RQD uses core pieces ≥ 10 cm; RQD > 90% = excellent.
P-waves are fastest; Rayleigh waves are slowest; S-waves do not pass through liquids.
Magnitude = energy (one value); intensity = damage (varies with place).
Richter scale introduced in 1935; open-ended; logarithmic.
Minimum 3 seismograph stations needed to locate an epicentre.
Pakistan seismic code – BCP SP-2007 (based on UBC-97); highest zone – 4 (Quetta).
Chaman Fault – transform fault; Makran – subduction zone.
Soft storey, short column and pounding are major causes of building collapse.
Lintel band is the most important band in masonry buildings.
